summary: Adds a PIM Join Attribute that identifies which topology to use when building a particular multicast distribution tree. This lets PIM signaling work with networks that keep several routing topologies at once. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A city may have separate road maps for cars and buses. This lets a router say which map to use when it sets up a delivery route for the same video to many viewers.

questions: how to select topology for multicast tree
what is the pim mt-id join attribute
subtitle: A PIM Join attribute that names which routing topology to use when building a multicast tree.

tldr.problem: PIM builds multicast trees using the routes of the network, but when a network keeps several topologies, PIM had no way to say which one a given tree should follow.
tldr.mechanism: A new PIM Join Attribute carries a numeric MT-ID that identifies the RPF topology to use, backed by a new Hello Option so routers can tell who supports it, plus rules for validating the attribute and resolving conflicts.
tldr.outcome: Trees for the same source can be built over separate network paths, which can make multicast more resilient to a single failure.

today: RFC 6420 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the PIM Join Attribute format of RFC 5384.

sections.title: Why Multicast Needs Topology Choice
sections.content:
Unicast protocols such as OSPF and IS-IS can present one network as several topologies. Multi-topology routing lets different traffic take different paths, or offers protection paths when something fails.

PIM uses Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) to build forwarding trees between multicast sources and receivers, using topology information from those routing protocols. The MT-ID Join Attribute lets PIM use the multiple topologies and build trees over separate paths even when the roots of the trees are the same.

The RFC's example is resilience. A stream can be duplicated and sent over two source trees, (S1, G1) and (S1, G2), built so they share no transit network segment. Then a single network failure does not cause any loss to the stream.

The RFC does not change the RPF check used when a packet is forwarded. How an application splits and merges streams is outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: If a city has a bus map and a car map, a delivery planner can pick a different map for each delivery. Two copies of the same video can then travel on completely different roads, so one traffic jam cannot stop both.

sections.title: RPF Topologies and the MT-ID
sections.content:
A PIM RPF topology is a collection of routes that PIM uses for RPF when it builds shared or source trees. The routes may come from different protocols. A source may be reachable in only one topology, or in several through different paths.

In the RFC's example, a source S is announced by MBGP and installed in every topology. Two unicast OSPF topologies, called OSPF 1000 and OSPF 2000, each contribute routes to a PIM topology, PIM 500 or PIM 600. A policy can say that G1 trees use PIM 500 and G2 trees use PIM 600, sending (S, G1) over S-R1-A-B-R2 and (S, G2) over S-R1-C-D-R2.

There are two ways to choose the topology: by configuration, or by putting the information in PIM Join packets as an attribute. Both can be used together, and the configured choice always takes precedence.

Each topology gets a unique numerical ID per PIM domain, the PIM MT-ID. It is only used by the PIM control plane. The forwarding plane tells topologies apart by group and/or source addresses. It need not equal the IGP's MT-ID, though using the same value is RECOMMENDED when one IGP supplies all the routes. The value 0 is reserved as the default and MUST NOT be included in the Join Attribute encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Each road map gets a number. The number is only used when planners talk to each other, and the trucks themselves are told apart by their addresses.

sections.title: Hello Option and Sending and Receiving
sections.content:
A router that supports the feature MUST include the PIM Join Attribute Option from RFC 5384 and the new PIM MT-ID Hello Option in its Hello packets. The attribute applies to Join and Assert packets used by PIM-SM, PIM-SSM and PIM-Bidir, not to other PIM packets.

When it originates a Join or Assert, a router may encode the MT-ID of the topology to use for RPF lookup. A router SHOULD NOT include the attribute if the MT-ID is 0, if the upstream router (or any router on the LAN) did not advertise the Join Attribute or MT-ID options, or for pruned sources.

On receipt, a router validates the encoding, resolves any conflict, and then uses the chosen topology for the RPF lookup unless local configuration says otherwise.

Older routers cope gracefully. One that supports RFC 5384 but not this document skips the unknown attribute and does not change its RPF decision. One that does not support RFC 5384 ignores the whole message, because it cannot parse the encoded sources.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers first tell each other whether they understand map numbers. A router only writes a map number on a delivery request if the next router said it understands them.

sections.title: Validation and Conflict Resolution
sections.content:
An upstream router does not need to know whether a downstream router supports the feature in order to accept the attribute. The validity checks are:

  • At most one MT-ID attribute is expected. If several appear, only the last one is accepted for that source.
  • The Length field must be 2. Otherwise the rest of the Join message, including the current entry, MUST be ignored.
  • The value MUST NOT be 0. If it is, the attribute is ignored and processing continues as if it were absent.

An upstream router has a conflict when it has no local topology policy and gets different MT-IDs from Joins or Asserts. It MUST follow the rules of RFC 5384 to select one, and it MAY ignore the Joins altogether to reduce the chance of transient forwarding loops. For Asserts it uses the tiebreaker rules of RFC 4601, and the MT-ID plays no part in picking the winner.

A downstream router that sees different MT-IDs in other routers' Joins MUST follow RFC 4601 as if the attribute did not exist, for example suppressing its own Join if one for the same (S,G) is seen. If its preferred upstream router loses the Assert and the winner uses a different MT-ID, it SHOULD still choose the winner as RPF neighbour but MUST NOT encode an MT-ID in Joins sent to it. Only the 12-bit Value field is compared.
sections.plainLanguage: If two requests name different maps, the router that does the work follows a fixed rule to pick one. Routers who are only watching ignore the map numbers and carry on as usual.

sections.title: Packet Formats
sections.content:
The PIM MT-ID Hello Option has OptionType 30 and OptionLength 0.

The MT-ID Join Attribute is a TLV with an F bit set to 0 (non-transitive), an E bit as specified in RFC 5384, an attribute type of 2, a Length of 2, 4 reserved bits set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt, and a Value that is the PIM MT-ID, 1 to 4095.

IANA assigned Hello Option type 30 under First Come First Served, with a Length of 0, and assigned value 2 in the PIM Join Attribute Types registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is just a tiny label: a few flag bits, a type, a length, and then the map number.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The security of the Join Attribute is only guaranteed by the security of the PIM packet that carries it, and the same is true of the Hello Option and the Hello packet. Malicious alteration of the MT-ID Hello Option or of the MT-ID in a packet might cause the PIM resiliency goals to be violated.

For that reason, the security considerations of RFC 4601 and RFC 5384 apply to these extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone sneaks in and changes the map number on a request, the delivery could go the wrong way. So the request has to be protected the same way as all the other PIM messages.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved; zero on transmission, ignored on receipt.
